---
title: "Appendix B — Tools and Datasets Cheat Sheet"
---

This appendix is a quick-reference index of the datasets and software libraries
used across the book. Each entry pairs a resource with a one-line statement of
what it is for and a link; where a resource has a citable primary source, the
name is followed by a citation to that source so the bibliography remains
self-contained. The lists are not exhaustive — they are the resources that recur
in the chapters, chosen because they are widely used, actively maintained, and
documented.

Two cautions apply to everything below. First, all of these resources are
*versioned*: sequences are added, structures are re-released, annotations are
revised, and libraries change APIs. A result is reproducible only if the release
or commit is recorded alongside the citation. Second, the links point to the
current live resource; when a paper and a database disagree, the database is the
authority for the data and the paper for the method.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Database, dataset, benchmark, library.** A *database* (UniProt, PDB) is a
curated, continuously updated store accessed by query. A *dataset* (a specific
GEO series) is a fixed collection used for a particular study. A *benchmark*
(TAPE, MoleculeNet) bundles several datasets with standardized tasks and metrics
so that models can be compared. A *library* (PyTorch, RDKit) is reusable software
rather than data.
:::

# Datasets

## Protein and Structure Databases

These resources supply the raw material for sequence and structure embeddings:
reference sequences and annotations, curated domain and fold families, and
experimentally determined or predicted coordinates. Most are updated on a regular
schedule, so version or release dates should be recorded when an analysis is
reported.

| Resource | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| UniProt [@uniprot2023uniprot] | Canonical protein sequences and functional annotation | <https://www.uniprot.org> |
| UniRef [@suzek2015uniref] | Clustered UniProt sequences for fast similarity search | <https://www.uniprot.org/help/uniref> |
| PDB [@berman2000protein] | Experimentally determined 3D structures | <https://www.rcsb.org> |
| Pfam [@mistry2021pfam] | Protein-family profile HMMs and domain annotations | <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/entry/pfam/> |
| CATH [@sillitoe2021cath] | Hierarchical classification of protein domains | <https://www.cathdb.info> |
| AlphaFold DB [@varadi2022alphafold] | Predicted structures for millions of proteins | <https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk> |

: Protein sequence and structure resources. {#tbl-protein-data}

## Genomics, Expression, and Atlases

Bulk and single-cell expression resources underpin the single-cell and
multi-omics chapters. They differ in scale (a few tissues vs. whole organisms),
in assay (RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq), and in whether raw reads or processed
matrices are distributed.

| Resource | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| GTEx [@lonsdale2013genotype] | Tissue-specific expression and expression QTLs | <https://gtexportal.org> |
| GEO [@barrett2013ncbi] | Archive of functional genomics datasets and series | <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/> |
| TCGA [@weinstein2013cancer] | Pan-cancer molecular profiles across tumor types | <https://www.cancer.gov/ccg/research/genome-sequencing/tcga> |
| ENCODE [@encode2012integrated] | Functional genomic elements and regulatory assays | <https://www.encodeproject.org> |
| Human Cell Atlas [@regev2017human] | Reference maps of human cell types and tissues | <https://www.humancellatlas.org> |
| Tabula Sapiens [@tabula2022tabula] | Multi-organ human single-cell transcriptomic atlas | <https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abl4896> |

: Expression and atlas resources. {#tbl-omics-data}

## Chemistry and Bioactivity

Small-molecule embeddings are trained and evaluated against curated bioactivity
and property data. These resources supply structures, assays, and protein–ligand
affinities; the benchmark entry bundles several of them into standard splits.

| Resource | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| ChEMBL [@gaulton2012chembl] | Curated bioactivity data for drug-like molecules | <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/> |
| PubChem [@kim2023pubchem] | Chemical structures, properties, and bioassays | <https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov> |
| PDBbind [@liu2015pdbwide] | Protein–ligand binding affinity measurements | <http://www.pdbbind.org.cn> |
| MoleculeNet [@wu2018moleculenet] | Benchmark datasets for molecular property prediction | <https://moleculenet.org> |

: Chemistry and bioactivity resources. {#tbl-chem-data}

## Networks, Pathways, and Graph Benchmarks

Relational data — protein interactions, pathways, and molecular graphs — is the
input to the graph-embedding methods. Pathway and interaction databases provide
the edges; graph benchmarks provide reproducible node-, edge-, and graph-level
tasks.

| Resource | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| STRING [@szklarczyk2021string] | Protein–protein interaction and association networks | <https://string-db.org> |
| Reactome [@gillespie2022reactome] | Curated pathway and reaction knowledgebase | <https://reactome.org> |
| KEGG [@kanehisa2023kegg] | Pathways, genomes, and disease maps | <https://www.genome.jp/kegg/> |
| OGB [@hu2020open] | Benchmarks for machine learning on graphs | <https://ogb.stanford.edu> |
| TAPE [@rao2019evaluating] | Benchmark suite for protein transfer learning | <https://github.com/songlab-cal/tape> |
| BEND [@marin2024bend] | Benchmark for DNA language models on genomic tasks | <https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12570> |

: Networks, pathways, and benchmark suites. {#tbl-network-data}

# Software Libraries

## Core Machine Learning

These frameworks provide tensors, automatic differentiation, optimizers, and
pretrained-model tooling. They are the substrate on which the embedding models in
the book are implemented; the trade-off is typically ecosystem and hardware
support versus flexibility.

| Library | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| PyTorch [@paszke2019pytorch] | Tensor computation with automatic differentiation | <https://pytorch.org> |
| Hugging Face Transformers [@wolf2020transformers] | Pretrained transformer models and tokenizers | <https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers> |
| scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011scikit] | Classical machine learning, PCA, and metrics | <https://scikit-learn.org> |
| Chemprop [@yang2019analyzing] | Directed message passing for molecular property prediction | <https://chemprop.readthedocs.io> |

: Core machine-learning libraries. {#tbl-ml-libs}

## Graph Learning

Graph neural networks are implemented with dedicated libraries that provide
message-passing primitives, mini-batching over graphs, and standard datasets.
They differ mainly in the underlying tensor framework and in their dataset and
sampling utilities.

| Library | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| PyTorch Geometric [@fey2019fast] | GNN layers and datasets built on PyTorch | <https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io> |
| Deep Graph Library (DGL) [@wang2019deep] | Graph-centric deep learning across frameworks | <https://www.dgl.ai> |

: Graph-learning libraries. {#tbl-graph-libs}

## Bioinformatics and Chemistry Toolkits

These libraries handle the non-ML parts of a pipeline: file formats, sequence and
structure algorithms, and cheminformatics descriptors and fingerprints.

| Library | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Biopython [@cock2009biopython] | Parsers and algorithms for molecular biology data | <https://biopython.org> |
| HMMER [@eddy2011accelerated] | Profile hidden Markov model sequence search | <http://hmmer.org> |
| TM-align [@zhang2005tmalign] | Protein structure alignment and TM-score | <https://zhanggroup.org/TM-align/> |
| RDKit [@rdkit] | Cheminformatics descriptors and fingerprints | <https://www.rdkit.org> |
| Open Babel [@oboyle2011open] | Chemical file-format conversion and tooling | <https://openbabel.org> |

: Bioinformatics and chemistry toolkits. {#tbl-bio-libs}

## Single-Cell Analysis

Single-cell pipelines combine data structures, preprocessing, probabilistic
latent-variable models, and visualization. The scverse ecosystem provides the
shared data format; the remaining libraries build on it.

| Library | Purpose | Link |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Scanpy [@wolf2018scanpy] | Scalable preprocessing, clustering, and visualization | <https://scanpy.readthedocs.io> |
| scvi-tools [@gayoso2022python] | Probabilistic models for single-cell omics | <https://scvi-tools.org> |
| scverse / AnnData [@virshup2023scverse] | Shared data structures for single-cell omics | <https://scverse.org> |

: Single-cell analysis libraries. {#tbl-sc-libs}

# Using These Resources

Datasets and benchmarks are only as trustworthy as the splits imposed on them.
For sequence and structure data, a random split that places homologous or
near-duplicate entries in both training and test sets inflates apparent
performance; grouped, time-based, or scaffold-based splits are the honest
alternative. For interaction and knowledge graphs, random edge splits can leak
information through the graph's complement. The evaluation chapter treats these
failure modes in detail [@rao2019evaluating; @wu2018moleculenet;
@hu2020open].

Formally, a supervised evaluation protocol partitions the labeled data into
disjoint training, validation, and test sets as in @eq-appb-split,

$$
\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \sqcup \mathcal{D}_{\text{val}} \sqcup \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}},
\qquad
\mathcal{D}_{a} \cap \mathcal{D}_{b} = \varnothing \;\; (a \neq b),
$$ {#eq-appb-split}

fits or selects $\theta$ using only $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ and
$\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}$, and estimates performance by the test empirical risk
of @eq-appb-leakage.

$$
\hat R_{\text{test}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}|}
\sum_{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i) \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}}
\ell\big(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i), y_i\big),
\qquad
\text{gap}(\theta) = R(\theta) - \hat R_{\text{test}}(\theta),
$$ {#eq-appb-leakage}

where $R(\theta)$ is the population risk. Leakage is exactly the condition
$\text{gap}(\theta) > 0$ systematically — the test set shares information with
the training set that would not be available for genuinely unseen entities — so
the estimated risk is optimistic and the split, not the model, is the source of
the error. The notation of @eq-appb-split and @eq-appb-leakage follows Appendix A.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Benchmark leakage.** *Leakage* is any dependence between the training and
evaluation data that lets a model exploit information it would not have on
genuinely unseen data. It is a property of the *split*, not of the model, and it
is the single most common reason a reported embedding performance does not
transfer.
:::

When reporting work built on these resources, record: the resource and release,
the license and any redistribution restrictions, the split strategy, and the
preprocessing steps (for example, which UniProt release or which GEO series
accession). Where a database offers a versioned, citable snapshot, cite that
rather than only the underlying paper, because a paper citation does not pin the
data.

# Where to Go Next

## Further Reading

- The UniProt, PDB, and Pfam release notes document schema changes between
  versions; record the release when reporting results [@uniprot2023uniprot;
  @berman2000protein; @mistry2021pfam].
- Luecken et al., "Benchmarking Atlas-level Data Integration in Single-cell
  Genomics" [@luecken2022benchmarking] — how to choose and evaluate integration
  methods on atlas-scale data.
- Rao et al., "Evaluating Protein Transfer Learning with TAPE"
  [@rao2019evaluating] — the design of a reproducible transfer-learning
  benchmark.
- Wu et al., "MoleculeNet" [@wu2018moleculenet] — dataset construction and splits
  for molecular machine learning.
- Wolf et al., "SCANPY" [@wolf2018scanpy] and Gayoso et al., "scvi-tools"
  [@gayoso2022python] — end-to-end single-cell analysis and probabilistic
  modeling workflows.
- For versioned, citable snapshots of databases, prefer the Zenodo record linked
  from each project's documentation; citations to the underlying paper alone do
  not pin the data release.
